problem: World-model + RL methods have mostly been applied to constrained manipulation/locomotion, and exploration for navigation typically needs expert data or goals; it is unclear whether world models with unsupervised curiosity can learn navigation from scratch in real, large and dynamic environments.
motivation: Exploration is the bottleneck of learned navigation, and data-efficient world models with intrinsic rewards look promising, but real-world robots face battery limits, drift, lighting changes and moved objects that simulation ignores. The paper studies how the approach scales from simulation to small and large real environments.
key_idea: Train a DreamerV2-style RSSM world model online from egocentric 64x64 RGB and learn an exploration policy in imagination using a Latent-Bayesian-Surprise (KL posterior vs. prior) intrinsic reward, deployed on a real TurtleBot with remote training and auto-docking.
insight: Coverage in simulation and the small controlled room is high because the world model predicts observations accurately, but in the large real lab the model keeps predicting stale object positions after objects are moved, so changes look like novel areas and curiosity keeps the agent revisiting the same vicinity. Qualitative prediction-vs-real comparisons (Fig. 4c) and the 60% coverage after 600k steps show world-model adaptability and the return-to-charger constraint, not the exploration objective, are the limiting factors.
method: World model: RSSM (deterministic GRU + discrete stochastic latents, DreamerV2) with CNN encoder/decoder, trained by ELBO on a replay buffer collected online
Curiosity reward: information gain approximated as KL between latent posterior and dynamics prior (Plan2Explore/LBS style)
Actor-critic in imagination: MLP exploration actor and critic trained on imagined rollouts (horizon 15) to maximise the intrinsic reward
Lifelong episodic training: N=500 steps per episode, then K=100 model updates on all collected episodes, then respawn/return to start

Real-robot pipeline: Kobuki TurtleBot 2i with Jetson AGX Orin, RealSense L515 depth for collision cancelling of forward moves, EKF (odometry+IMU+LiDAR) auto-docking, episodes uploaded and trained on a remote GTX 1080 server

setting.backbone: DreamerV2-style RSSM world model + MLP actor-critic (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Online self-collected exploration data only: 2M steps in sim per apartment; up to 140k steps (small real) and 600k steps (large real); no expert data
setting.observation: egocentric monocular 64x64 RGB (depth used only for collision avoidance on real robot)
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: forward 0.25 m, turn left/right 10°
setting.privileged: none for the policy; ground-truth positions used only to compute coverage metrics

numbers_note: Coverage results are given only in figures (Fig. 2 for Habitat vs C-BET); text gives only approximate real-world numbers (>80% coverage in 140k steps small room, 60% in 600k steps large lab), no standard navigation benchmark metrics. Auto-docking success: 96% small (572/596), 74% large (758/1023).
results: In three Habitat Replica apartments the agent (2M steps) achieves higher exploration coverage and efficiency than C-BET (5M steps), which revisits areas. On the real TurtleBot it reaches over 80% coverage of a 2x4 m room in 140k steps but only about 60% coverage of a 10x23 m lab after 600k steps.
limitations: World model does not adapt to moved objects/lighting changes, treating them as novel areas and causing repeated exploration

Battery limit (~10 min) and return-to-dock requirement plus odometry drift (74% docking success in large space) limit coverage; the paper evaluates only coverage, not goal-directed navigation, with few runs and no numeric tables
